paragraphs.text: Recently a group of researchers concluded that our planet's ecosystems have a net worth of about $33 trillion a year. The main purpose of putting a price tag on the Earth's natural resources was to dramatize the importance of preserving the environment long into the future. While it seems like a modern problem, saving the planet is actually a centuries-old challenge, particularly as it relates to marine environments. For example, there is evidence that fisheries in ancient times caused a significant decrease in marine species. Certainly by the 1300s in Europe, a successful and growing market for fish, as well as other developments like changing agricultural practices, forced species such as salmon and sturgeon into decline.

The 1800s saw an increase in hunting fish, seals and whales, thanks to the development of steam and then oil-powered fishing vessels. Open seawhaling began in the early 20th century; the development of explosive harpoons, the ability to process whales at sea, and the strong demand for margarine made from whale oil all contributed to dramatic rises in catches. A wide-ranging decline in whale populations took place from the largest, most valuable species (e.g. blue whale) through to the smallest species (minke whale).

Over the same period, as fishing Deets greatly expanded and increasingly powerful fishing vessels came into use, improved technologies for navigating and catching fish led to greater pressure on fish stocks and the marine ecosystems. Later, in 1908, after analyzing catch statistics from the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), further evidence came in 2003 when a group of scientists identified a global shift in fish catches, from large long-lived species to mainly short-lived creatures such as shellfish. Aside from these problems caused by overfishing, evidence was building that ocean creatures were becoming more vulnerable to shocks, such as invasions by alien species and climate-change effects.

Further evidence came in 2003 when a scientific study was conducted to document how sharks, seabirds and turtles were suffering large-scale declines as they became accidental victims, 'by-catch', of many industrial fisheries. Scientists also began to document the great harm that modern fishing methods caused to cold-water coral communities.

While research on overfishing has now demonstrated that fish stocks can recover if levels of fishing are reduced, it's clear that in many parts of the world's oceans this is not happening. Indeed these studies started a major debate between marine ecologists, biologists and fishing industry executives, as global yields from marine capture fisheries are continually decreasing. By-catch of some marine animals, such as albatrosses, still poses a threat of extinction. Habitat destruction resulting from fishing has not been stopped.

In addition to overfishing, other human activities are damaging marine ecosystems. During the 1960 and 1970s, several major accidents with oil tankers resulted in serious oil spills. And while oil pollution is still a significant problem, other less visible sources of pollution are also causing large-scale damage to the ocean.

Persistent organic pollutant as well as heavy metals such as mercury are being recognized as major health issues for marine animals (especially large species, such as killer whales and tuna) and also for humans. The oceans are becoming the dumping ground for a wide range of chemicals that leach out of all manner of plastics that are floating in our seas. Farming chemicals are pouring into the oceans through rivers; in some cases these artificially fertilize waters on the coast, producing bloom of algae which bring in bacteria that break it down. This process produces a layer of green slime, which depletes the water of oxygen and creates dead zones.

Our release of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2), is leading to a profound disturbance in ocean temperatures and ocean chemistry. Since the late 1970s, mass coral bleaching from ocean warming has killed large areas of tropical coral reefs. Marine animals are experiencing changes in how species are distributed, as well as when the stages of their life cycles take place, sometimes with severely damaging effects across the wider ecosystem. Such effects often originate in the lower levels of the food chain and move up through to larger animals such as fish and seabirds. The oceans are becoming increasingly acidic, which affects the growth rates of animals with calcium carbonate shell or skeletons, and has other negative impacts on the bodies of sea animals.

Knowledge of these ever-increasing threats to marine ecosystems leads to a clear call for action. This includes better conservation management and new technology to support conservation efforts. With such, not only might we save our precious marine life, but we may also be saved by it: our oceans' untapped minerals, genes, proteins and other biomolecules are likely to furnish the medicines of our future.
